title: Search a 2D Matrix
description: Brute force to optimized: scanning every cell versus binary search over a virtual flattened 1D index.

blocks.text: Problem Summary: Given an m x n matrix where each row is sorted in ascending order, and the first integer of each row is greater than the last integer of the previous row, return true if target exists in the matrix, or false otherwise, in O(log(m times n)) time.

blocks.caption: What goes in, what comes out

blocks.content: {"headers":["Aspect","Detail"],"rows":[["Input","matrix (m rows, n columns, sorted as described), target"],["Output","true if target exists anywhere in the matrix, false otherwise"],["Goal","Achieve O(log(m*n)) by treating the matrix as one virtual sorted 1D array"],["Constraints","1 <= m, n <= 100"]]}

{"headers":["Signal in the problem","Pattern it points to"],"rows":[["\"Each row sorted, and rows themselves in increasing order relative to each other\"","The entire matrix, read row by row, is equivalent to one single sorted 1D array"],["\"O(log(m*n)) required\"","Standard binary search over a virtual index space spanning the whole matrix"]]}

blocks.text: Because every row is individually sorted, and each row's first element exceeds the previous row's last element, reading the matrix left-to-right, top-to-bottom produces one single, fully sorted sequence of m times n values. This means the entire 2D search problem can be treated as a standard 1D binary search.

blocks.title: Analogy: A Sorted List Wrapped Onto Multiple Shelves
blocks.text: Picture a single long sorted list of books, but physically arranged across several shelves, filling each shelf left to right before moving to the next. Even though the books are split across shelves, the overall order is still perfectly sorted, so the same binary search strategy used for a single shelf still works, just with a small conversion from "position in the list" to "which shelf and which spot."

blocks.caption: Reading the matrix row by row produces one single sorted 1D array, enabling standard binary search

blocks.text: Result: true. Flattened, the matrix reads [1,3,5,7,10,11,16,20,23,30,34,60], and 3 is present.

Before searching row by row (which would still need a per-row binary search, O(m log n)), notice that the matrix's described sorted structure means it behaves EXACTLY like one flat sorted array of size m*n, and standard binary search applies directly once each virtual 1D index is converted to a (row, column) pair.

blocks.title: Building the Intuition
blocks.text:
Observation 1: If the matrix were physically flattened row by row into one array, that array would be fully sorted, given the problem's guarantees about row order and row-to-row ordering.

Observation 2: Binary search over a virtual index range [0, m*n - 1] works exactly as it would over a real 1D array, just needing a way to map a virtual index back to its actual (row, column) position.

Observation 3: For a 0-indexed virtual index i in a matrix with n columns, the row is i divided by n (integer division), and the column is i modulo n.

Observation 4: This mapping lets a single binary search over the virtual index directly answer whether target exists, in O(log(m*n)) total.
This leads to binary searching over a virtual index range [0, m*n-1], converting each candidate index to its (row, column) via integer division and modulo, and comparing that cell's value to target.
Scan every cell of the matrix directly, comparing each to target.

items: Iterate over every row and every column.
If matrix[row][col] equals target, return true.
If the scan completes without a match, return false.

blocks.text: Why the code is written this way

items: A direct nested scan checks every cell, correct regardless of any sorted structure.
This costs O(m times n), ignoring the sorted structure entirely, which allows O(log(m*n)) instead.

blocks.text: Limitation: the described sorted structure means the matrix is equivalent to one flat sorted array; binary search over a virtual 1D index achieves O(log(m*n)) instead.

blocks.title: The Optimization Journey
blocks.text:
Why row-by-row scanning is unnecessary: given the matrix's sorted guarantees, it behaves identically to a single flat sorted array, just physically laid out in rows.

The virtual-index trick: binary search over indices 0 to m*n-1 exactly as if this were a real 1D array; the only extra step is converting a virtual index i to its actual (row, column) via row = i // n, column = i % n.

Applying the comparison: fetch matrix[row][column] for the candidate virtual index, compare it to target, and narrow the binary search range exactly as in standard 1D binary search.

The core idea: standard binary search over a virtual flattened index space, with a simple row/column conversion at each step.
Binary search over virtual index range [0, m*n-1]. At each step, convert the midpoint to (row, column), compare matrix[row][column] to target, and narrow the range accordingly.

blocks.caption: Binary search a virtual flattened index, converting to (row, column) at each step

blocks.text: Since the matrix's rows are individually sorted and ordered relative to each other exactly as the problem guarantees, reading it row by row produces one single, fully sorted sequence. Mapping a virtual 1D index i to (i // n, i % n) correctly recovers the value at that position in this equivalent flattened sequence, so standard binary search applies unchanged, just with this small index-conversion step at each comparison.

blocks.text: Search a 2D Matrix demonstrates that a matrix with strong enough sorted guarantees is really just a 1D sorted array in disguise, and standard binary search applies directly with a simple index-to-coordinate conversion.

items: Using row/column division and modulo in the wrong order (row = mid // n, col = mid % n, not the reverse).
Confusing this problem with Search a 2D Matrix II (where rows and columns are each sorted independently but NOT globally ordered), which requires a different technique (staircase search).

blocks.title: If The Interviewer Says This, Think This
blocks.text: If the interviewer says "each row sorted, and rows collectively ordered too", think: treat the whole matrix as one flattened 1D sorted array, binary search directly.

items: How would this differ if only rows AND columns were independently sorted, without the global row-ordering guarantee (Search a 2D Matrix II)?
How would you find the position of the FIRST or LAST occurrence if duplicates were allowed?

Any problem where a multi-dimensional structure secretly behaves as a 1D sorted sequence.

blocks.title: Complexity Summary
blocks.text: The full cell scan runs in O(m times n) time; the virtual-index binary search runs in O(log(m times n)) time, both using O(1) space.

items: Pattern: binary search over a virtual flattened 1D index, converting to (row, column) at each step.
Core Idea: treat the matrix as one sorted 1D array of size m*n; binary search it directly, mapping each virtual index via integer division and modulo.
Time: O(m times n) for the full scan, O(log(m times n)) for the optimized binary search.
Most Important Observation: the matrix's sorted guarantees mean it is functionally identical to a single flat sorted array.
Interview Difficulty: an accessible extension of standard binary search to a 2D structure.
One line memory trick: binary search a virtual index; row = index/n, col = index%n.
